Q: Pygame 2D image animations rendering in the wrong way A:

As you can see, the flipping is working fine - What happens is that the base coordinate point, from which your character is drawn, are the coordinates that are on the top-left of your character image.

(sorry, reading your code -it is the point

So, when it is facing right, these are some point behind the character back, and the sword seems to point forward. When flipping the character, this point will be at the left at the sword tip - and the character body will appear to be pushed to the right by the length of the sword.

What you need to to is to add a negative offset of a few pixels to the character position when drawing it, which would compensate the sword length if it extends to the left.

You should put in your character (it can be in the init), a mapping of which frames, and which action, and which flip state, the offset should be - and then, upon drawing it, add that offset to the self.rect:

self.offsets = {}
# your current example will need this:
self.offsets["attack", 0, True] = pygame.Vector2(-10, 0) # trying 10 pixels here, you might want to fine tune this number
# Add other entries if needed
...

Eventually, you could put that data in a text file, alongside your code, and parse it when initializing the game: that would allow another person, designing the sprites, to input the correct offsets for you, without having to hardcode that in the the Python code.

And then, to use these offsets, at the animate method, bellow the match block you could add:

match self.animation_state:
    ...

self.rect.topleft += self.offsets.get(
        (self.animation_state, int(self.animation_index), self.flip),
         pygame.Vector2(0, 0)
    )

the other option

As you game coding skills progress, you may find that you could possibly track the sword as a "separate" equipement from the main character - that would allow you to track only the character coordinates, and draw the equipment separately, with coordinates relative to the character instead. It is easy to perceive this adds a whole new level of complexity, that is why I didn't mention it earlier - but also a new level of correctness. And nonetheless, keeping track of the equipment as a separate item is one thing, rendering it correctly is still another challenge for 2D overlaying sprites like in this case. 3D games could let the game engine take care of that - but that is not the case here.

Q: What executable format does NTLDR use? How is it loaded into memory and executed? A:

NTLDR is laid out in a bespoke format without any headers or magic numbers that specifically identify it or define its structure. It consists of two parts: a 16-bit stub loader (STARTUP.COM) and a PE32/COFF binary (OSLOADER.EXE) appended to it. The former performs initial hardware detection and provides the latter with callbacks giving access to boot-time services like BIOS interrupt calls. The offset where OSLOADER begins is not stored in an easily-accessible location (the address is hardcoded within the stub portion’s code) and has to be determined by probing magic numbers; in all Windows versions I checked, OSLOADER.EXE begins at a 16-byte aligned offset somewhere around 16~20 KiB into the NTLDR file. Up to Windows 2000 (NT 5.0), the COFF portion of NTLDR did not contain an MZ stub or a PE32 magic number – a COFF architecture identifier for x86 (0x14c) appears directly after STARTUP.COM. In Windows XP, the embedded OSLOADER.EXE became a full PE32 file, including a DOS stub (even if there is no way the stub will ever be executed).

The STARTUP.COM loader has two entry points, chosen depending on the file system booted from:

  • The FAT12 and FAT16 boot sector loads a single sector of NTLDR at address 2000:0000 and transfers control to address 2000:0003, so that it can load the rest. Execution then continues from 2000:0000.
  • For other file systems, boot area code loads the entirety of NTLDR in one go at address 2000:0000 and transfers control there directly.

There are versions of the stub loader that tolerate being placed at other addresses – like the PXE-capable version, STARTROM.COM – but those will also eventually relocate themselves to segment 0x2000.

The loading protocol also requires that the DL register contain the unit number of the boot device (i.e. the drive number used with interrupt 0x13 services) and that 0000:7c00 contain the contents of the partition’s boot sector (see https://retrocomputing.stackexchange.com/a/31394/15334 for how it is used).

The same basic protocol and bipartite structure remains in the PC BIOS version of BOOTMGR of Windows Vista and later – although the attached PE binary (BOOTMGR.EXE) may be compressed, aligned at a finer boundary, and its loading protocol is different.

Q: searching YouTube for videos with specific range of views eg. between 9,000,000 and 11,000,000 A:

First off, you would need the Youtube Data API. "v3" means nothing because it's simply the current version, like "Windows 10."

The API lets you get a video's view count, but doesn't put it in a range like 9 million to 11 million.

Youtube's own search function is pretty sophisticated. For instance, https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=movie+trailer&search_sort=video_view_count&filters=month. This gives all results for "movie trailer," within the last month, sorted by view count. You can customize the URL, i.e. "week" instead of month would return only trailers from the last week. Or year, etc. Essentially this is a "Videos: List: MostPopular" query, with subject filter.

I have a few Youtube API scripts, and I hardly think it's worth the hassle to do it that way when Youtube's advanced search get you 99% there. If you did, you would need to to a Search:list query for a given subject (i.e. "movie trailer"). Limited to a given time frame (i.e. last month). Then for each video ID, make a Videos:list query to get its view count. Then print all, sorted by views.
